name: Upright piano (Knight)
note: An instrument recipe for the sampler (doc 24, Instruments, Sample preparation and Sampler rules). It describes exactly the files the prep step produced; nothing here is a tuning choice. type, id, name, version: what this is. source: where the recordings come from (library, folder url, license) and what the library's own note files say (notes). channels: channel count of every file. formats: each file exists once per format under root, as <file>.ogg (Ogg Opus, 48 kHz, 96 kbps stereo or 64 kbps mono, variable bitrate) and <file>.m4a (AAC-LC at the source rate, 128 kbps stereo or 96 kbps mono); the browser picks the first it can play. root: folder of the files, relative to the repo. layers: the number of velocity layers in the sustain set, layer 1 the quietest. sets: one entry per articulation: sus (sustain, pedal down or natural ring), nosus (dampers working), rel (release or key-off noise, played on note-off), pedal (sounds of the pedal mechanism). Each set has source (the library subfolder) and zones; a zone is one recorded key: note (scientific pitch, C4 = middle C, sharps written s in file names), midi (C4 = 60). measuredCents: the zone's measured pitch offset from 12-tone equal temperament at A4 = 440 Hz, in cents, as recorded; piano strings are inharmonic (partial n sits at n f0 sqrt(1 + B n^2)), so it is fitted from partials 1 to 6 (2 to 8 in the bass, where the fundamental is weak) over a window of the early sustain, each partial taken as the level-weighted centre of its unison-string cluster, and it is the pitch of the fitted first partial. Real pianos are stretch-tuned on purpose (bass flat, treble sharp); nothing has been corrected. tuneLayer: the layer the zone's number comes from (the middle one). tuneResidualCents: how far the found partials sit from the fit (root mean square, cents). tunePartials: which partials were found and used. layerSpreadCents: the largest difference between this zone's layers. inharmonicityB: the fitted B. unisonSplitCents: the widest spread seen inside one partial's cluster (a sign of unison strings tuned apart, which is heard as beating or chorus). tuneConfidence: 0 to 1, falls with fewer partials, a larger residual and a larger layer spread; below about 0.5 trust the ear over the number. layers: the files of the zone, quietest first; file is the path under root without extension; layer is its velocity layer and rr its round-robin take when the set has takes. peakDb: the file's sample peak in dBFS. attackRmsDb: the RMS level of its first 300 ms after the onset, in dBFS. Whether these levels mean anything depends on the source (see levels below). brightness: the share of energy above 1.5 times the note's fundamental (or 1 kHz, whichever is higher) in those first 300 ms, which should rise from layer to layer; in a very quiet file the noise floor can inflate it. lenS: length after the prep, in seconds. trimStartMs: how much was cut from the start (the onset, the first point above -50 dB of the file's peak, is kept with 3 ms before it). measuredCents on a layer is that file's own measurement. src: the original file name. Every file was cut where its 50 ms RMS fell to 60 dB below its peak, or at a maximum length (8 s at A0 falling evenly per semitone to 4 s at C8 for sustains, 2 s for releases), whichever came first, then given an equal-power fade over its last 250 ms (100 ms for releases and pedal sounds) so it ends in true silence. No gain was changed. levels: whether the source normalised each file (normalized true: the levels say nothing about how hard the key was played, so the sampler rebuilds the dynamic range from velocity with its own curve and must not re-gain the layers) or kept the recorded levels (normalized false: the layers already step up in level as they were played, and the sampler should play them at their own level). range: the lowest and highest sustain zone. problems: anything odd found while preparing, in plain words. The .m4a files decode about 23 ms longer than the .ogg files because AAC pads its last frame with silence; the start is in the same place in both. Knight: pedal files list kind (down = pedal pressed, from Pedal/On; up = pedal released, from Pedal/Off; both confirmed by the waveform: down files ring on for seconds, up files decay to silence), events (number of separate knocks found at -20 dB of the file's peak) and centroidHz (the spectral centre, a rough measure of how thuddy it sounds). The pedal files keep their whole natural length.

source.notes: Folder 'Upright Piano, Knight'. Info.txt says it was sampled by Simon Dalzell of Ivy Audio for the VSCO 2 Pro sample set, that the included chart gives the tag (left) for the MIDI key (right), and that the instrument was sampled in a whole-tone scale starting from the low A of the instrument. PitchValueConversionChart.txt maps tags 000 to 044 to MIDI keys 21, 23, 25 ... 107, 108 (A0 then every whole tone to B7, then C8). The files, however, are not tagged 000 to 044: they carry note names (A-1, B-1, C#0 ... B6, C7) that are one octave low against scientific pitch. Mapping used: the 45 distinct note tags were sorted by the pitch they name and paired in order with chart entries 000 to 044, which gives A-1 = 21 (A0), B-1 = 23 (B0), C#0 = 25 (C#1) ... B6 = 107 (B7), C7 = 108 (C8); this is the same as adding one octave to every name, and the last step (B to C, one semitone) matches the chart's 107 to 108. Pitch measurement confirmed it on every zone. Sustains: two velocity layers vl1 and vl2, one round robin. Releases: one file per zone (Player_rel_rr1_<note>), no layers. Pedal: four recordings in Pedal/On (pedal pressed: dampers lift, the hit is followed by a long ring of the undamped strings) and four in Pedal/Off (pedal released: dampers land, a thud then decay to the noise floor); every one is kept, as pedal/down-1..4 and pedal/up-1..4.

levels.note: Recorded levels kept: v1 peaks near -11 to -29 dBFS, v2 near -5 to -24 dBFS. Play the layers at their own level.

problems: sus: brightness does not rise with layer in 1 of 45 zones: B7 (v1 0.000, v2 0.000)

sus: layers of the same key disagree in pitch by more than 5 cents in 2 zones (usually a high, fast-dying note or a unison that beats; the zone number uses the middle layer): A6 (v1 +23.5, v2 +7.6); B6 (v1 +15.5, v2 +8.6)

5 sustain files end in the source before falling to -60 dB or reaching the maximum length, so the 250 ms fade lands on a still-audible tail (tail level when the file ends: -57.6 to -52.4 dB below peak): sus/A7-v1 (2.39 s), sus/Ds7-v1 (3.134 s), sus/F7-v1 (2.522 s), sus/G7-v1 (2.348 s), sus/F7-v2 (2.74 s)

sus/B7-v1 (Player_vl1_rr1_B6.wav): pitch check flagged it; reviewed by hand: sounds about 62 cents above B7 (4094 Hz). C8 is also about 62 cents sharp and A7 37, G7 32, F7 26, so this is the top of a steep stretch tuning rather than a wrong file, but these two keys sit closer to a quarter tone sharp than any other zone; trust the ear
sus/C8-v1 (Player_vl1_rr1_C7.wav): pitch check flagged it; reviewed by hand: about 62 cents sharp of C8 (4348 Hz); see B7
sus/B7-v2 (Player_vl2_rr1_B6.wav): pitch check flagged it; reviewed by hand: same as v1, about 62 cents sharp of B7
sus/C8-v2 (Player_vl2_rr1_C7.wav): pitch check flagged it; reviewed by hand: about 64 cents sharp of C8; see B7

onset check: in 39 encoded files the -30 dB threshold crossing moved by more than 2 ms after encoding (codec ripple on a slow, quiet attack); cross-correlation of the first 80 ms against the processed WAV shows no shift in any of them (lag 0 to 0.02 ms), so the starts are in place
